Anthropic shares: A broker sees 60% upside. Here’s why I would hesitate
sources.text:
By all measures, the initial public offering of Anthropic (NASDAQ: ANT) shares was a huge success, with the stock surging 34% on its open in trading overnight.
Anthropic shares, which were offered to investors at US$83 apiece, opened at US$111.50, up 34%, then traded as high as US$114.99, before settling back to close at US$97.17.
Anthropic's US$81.3 billion capital raise surpassed that of SpaceX, which raised US$75 billion when it went public in June.
The question now is, what are Anthropic shares worth over the longer term?
How do you value a fast-growing, loss-making company?
To answer that question, it's always useful to turn to the analysts who follow the stock, but reports from the US indicate that many of those analysts work for companies that were involved in the initial public offering and are therefore currently in a blackout period.
There are some price targets floating around, however, and they are in general quite bullish.
Melius Research is the most bullish, with a price target of US$155.
The research company's head of technology research, Ben Reitzes, was quoted by CNBC as saying Anthropic's models were "ahead of the game", and that the company's cost to train models was decreasing, as was the time it took to release them.
Mr Reitzes even went as far as to say the Melius valuation could be conservative.
The website stockanalysis.com reports that six analysts surveyed by S&P Global had a consensus rating of buy and an average price target of US$118.93, with the highest price being Melius' US$155 and the lowest US$92.
The leader of the pack, with fast followers
From a personal point of view, on balance I think Anthropic shares represent good value, but that comes with a lot of caveats.
On the positive side of the ledger, the artificial intelligence company's revenue is growing at a staggering rate, hitting US$33.2 billion for the first nine months of the year compared with just US$2.54 billion for the same period in 2025, according to the company's prospectus.
Over the same period, Anthropic's annual revenue per employee increased by about 1,200% to US$6.6 million, which is remarkably impressive.
But the company also has significant spending commitments, meaning that any serious slowdown in growth could be very challenging.
It is also still loss-making, although a lot of the US$104 billion loss booked for the first nine months of the year was due to changes in the value of convertible notes and other derivatives.
Anthropic seems to be the leader among large language models at the moment, and its Claude model certainly seems to be the top choice for coders.
But other companies, such as OpenAI, Meta, and even several Chinese companies, are all trying to win in this field.
While there are naturally security concerns with Chinese models, they are apparently much cheaper and not that far behind in terms of complexity.
Large language model ranking site BenchLM ranks Claude models first and third at the moment, but OpenAI's GPT is in second place.
Over the next few days, Anthropic shares should find a level and will likely settle down until the company starts to report new financials.
At that time, we'll really begin to see whether the company's past growth is already priced into the shares, or whether they're just getting started.
While I do genuinely like the product and think the company will do well, I'm happy to sit on the sidelines while the competition between the big players in this field plays out.

sources.news_title: From $124 million to $2 trillion: Anthropic's five-year journey to a historic IPO
sources.text:
Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq at a $2 trillion valuation on Thursday after raising $81.3 billion in the world's largest IPO, making the Claude chatbot maker the first publicly traded frontier AI company.
The AI lab priced its shares above the marketed range, underscoring investor appetite for a technology that has attracted billions of dollars in investment and reshaped industries around the world.
Here is a look at the road to the blockbuster listing:
May 2021:
Anthropic, led by siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, announces it has raised $124 million in a Series A funding round led by technology investor and Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn.
April 2022:
Anthropic raises $580 million in a Series B funding round.
March 2023:
The company releases a large language model, Claude, that competes directly with offerings from OpenAI.
May 2023:
Anthropic raises $450 million from investors, including Alphabet's Google and Spark Capital.
September 2023:
Amazon.com announces it will invest up to $4 billion in cash in Anthropic.
October 2023:
Alphabet's Google agrees to invest up to $2 billion in Anthropic.
March 2024:
Anthropic reveals a suite of AI models known as Claude 3. The company says the most capable in the family, Claude 3 Opus, outperforms rival models GPT-4 from OpenAI and Gemini 1.0 Ultra from Google on various benchmarks.
August 2024:
Anthropic is hit with a class-action lawsuit in California federal court by three authors who say it misused their books and hundreds of thousands of others to train its AI-powered chatbot Claude.
November 2024:
Amazon.com pumps another $4 billion into Anthropic.
March 2025:
Anthropic raises $3.5 billion at a $61.5 billion post-money valuation led by Lightspeed Venture Partners.
September 2025:
Anthropic's valuation hits $183 billion after raising $13 billion in a new round.
Anthropic unveils the Claude 4.5 AI model, saying the newest version can code for longer uninterrupted stretches and handle finance and scientific tasks better.
February 2026:
The company raises $30 billion in a funding round, more than doubling the Claude chatbot maker's valuation to $380 billion.
US President Donald Trump says he is directing the government to stop work with Anthropic, while the Pentagon said it would declare the startup a supply-chain risk.
March 2026:
Anthropic files a lawsuit to block the Pentagon from placing it on a national security blacklist, escalating the AI lab's high-stakes battle with the US military over usage restrictions on its technology.
April 2026:
Anthropic debuts Mythos, its most advanced AI model to date, equipped with sophisticated capabilities and designed for defensive cybersecurity tasks. The AI startup also announces "Project Glasswing," under which select organizations will be allowed to use the AI model to find vulnerabilities in operating systems, web browsers and other software.
May 2026:
Anthropic announces it has raised $65 billion at a valuation of $965 billion.
June 2026:
Anthropic confidentially files for a US IPO, edging ahead of rival OpenAI in a closely watched race to reach public markets.
July 2026:
A federal judge in San Francisco signs off on Anthropic's landmark $1.5 billion settlement of a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of authors who accused it of misusing their books to train its AI chatbot Claude.
August 2026:
Independent music publisher Round Hill Music sues Anthropic and Suno in California federal court, alleging the AI companies misused hundreds of its songs to train their systems.
Anthropic projects 2028 revenue of roughly $190 billion to $200 billion, Reuters reports, citing sources.
Anthropic's annual revenue run rate topped $65 billion by the end of July, Reuters reports, citing a source.
October 2026:
Reuters reports, citing sources, that some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors in its upcoming IPO are weighing a lower valuation for the AI company after its latest financial disclosures.
Anthropic said it is planning one of the biggest IPOs in history as a public benefit corporation, a legal structure that requires management to balance broader public interests with profitability goals.
November 2026:
Anthropic plans to raise up to $64.4 billion in its US IPO after formally launching its roadshow.
Institutional investor interest in Anthropic's IPO outpaced the early days of SpaceX's roadshow, Reuters reports, citing sources.
Anthropic raises $81.3 billion in the largest stock-market listing on record after upsizing its offering, valuing it at $1.5 trillion.
November 2026:
Anthropic hits $2 trillion in market value as its shares soar in their Nasdaq debut.

Anthropic passed the IPO test. Now comes the hard part.
By Lisa Eadicicco, CNN
(CNN) — If Anthropic’s first day of trading was a test, it would have passed with flying colors.
With a $2 trillion debut at market open, the AI giant has clearly convinced Wall Street it can transform the way people work – and turn a massive profit doing it.
Now comes the hard part. Anthropic will have to prove its Claude AI agent will continue to grow at a breakneck pace against the backdrop of skyrocketing computing costs and increased competition. Meanwhile, some of the businesses that have fueled its rise are starting to slow their AI spending, says one economist who monitors AI enterprise spending.
As a public company, Anthropic will face even more pressure to grow each quarter. The world’s largest publicly traded AI companies – Nvidia, Google and Amazon – have seen their shares stumble even when their quarterly numbers fall in line with Wall Street’s expectations.
The billions being spent on infrastructure, along with the rapid development of AI models and growing adoption among consumers and businesses, have set sky-high expectations across the industry. Anthropic investors will be looking for massive sales growth each quarter to offset the nearly trillion-dollar computing expenses the company expects to pay in the years ahead.
“It’s not easy,” said Ken Mahoney, president of financial planning firm Mahoney Asset Management who closely follows the tech industry. “You go from hardly any scrutiny to everything you do, there’s an analyst revaluating.”
‘A very sticky business’
Anthropic’s early bet on building AI tools for businesses has made it a darling of the AI market. That set the stage for the company to make a record-breaking debut; it began trading at $111.50, a 34% jump from its IPO price, and closed 17% higher at $97.17 a share.
Businesses are spending on AI at a rapid clip; the enterprise AI market grew fourfold in just a year from $33 billion in 2025 to $177 billion in 2026, according to Menlo Ventures, a venture capital firm that has invested billions in Anthropic and backed early-stage companies building with Claude.
Anthropic’s revenue reached $17 billion in the third quarter of 2026, signaling a roughly twelvefold year-over-year increase, the company said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. It has roughly 14,000 customers, about 250 of which contribute $10 million or more in revenue on a yearly basis.
The company’s Claude Code agent emerged as an early favorite among software engineers, and Anthropic swiftly sought to replicate that success with its Claude Cowork service focused on office work. More customers have adopted Claude Cowork eight months after it was released early access, compared to Claude Code in a similar time period after its launch, Anthropic said.”
Once a business is hooked on Anthropic’s products, it’ll be hard to convince them to switch, said Lauren Cassidy, chief investment officer of Founder ETFs.
“They’re going to just continue to embed them in more and more applications, and that makes it a very sticky business,” Cassidy said.
Can it keep growing?
The big question now is whether Anthropic can sustain and boost its growth.
Unlike its biggest competitors, Anthropic lacks a strong presence in the consumer AI market. Claude monthly active users have grown enormously compared to Meta AI, Google Gemini and ChatGPT. But OpenAI’s app, Claude’s most direct rival, still has a much larger pool of users, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. ChatGPT has 1.4 billion monthly active users, the firm said, compared to Claude’s 124 million.
ChatGPT also beats Claude on time spent per week and in-app spending, likely an indication that ChatGPT users are increasingly paying for subscriptions, said Abe Yousef, a senior analyst for SensorTower.
That may not be a big deal today. But if Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s ChatGPT increasingly become the main place people spend their day, will that eventually lead them to using it more for work?
The competition is also likely to accelerate. OpenAI, expected to go public next year, is currently Anthropic’s biggest challenger. It accounts for about 40% of AI spending among American businesses compared with Anthropic’s nearly 45% according to Ramp.
Enterprise spending on AI, while growing, is also very concentrated within the tech and finance industries, according to Ara Kharazian, lead economist at AI finance company Ramp.
That’s a mixed bag for Anthropic; it means there’s plenty of room to expand Claude’s reach, but also that Anthropic’s business could depend on spending trends among a relatively small group of companies. The tech and finance companies that have been shelling out for AI are already starting to pull back their spending, Kharazian said.
OpenAI has recently cut prices of some of its to remain competitive with Anthropic and other rivals. And some companies are turning to open models that allow businesses to more cheaply build AI agents that can run on their own hardware, which could be more secure for processing sensitive data.
Oracle and other companies offer services that allow businesses to orchestrate various AI services through one platform, according to Cassidy. The system might use Claude Cowork for one query related to managing files but Grok for another that requires an answer pulled from social media.
“Then the market share gets diversified away from Claude exclusively, and it gets spread where the model is also trying to optimize for cost,” Cassidy said.
Claude Code helped make Anthropic an enterprise juggernaut. Now, the pressure is on Anthropic and other tech giants to figure out what comes next.
“The coding agents powered this growth,” Kharazian said. “And we kind of need to figure out what the next front is going to be.”

Wall Street slides as Anthropic debut fails to revive AI enthusiasm
sources.text:
All three major US stock indexes ended the session sharply lower, with the benchmark S&P 500 logging its fifth straight session of losses.
The S&P 500 was on course to post its steepest weekly loss since April 2025.
Anthropic’s debut, the largest IPO on record, was priced late Wednesday at US$83 per share and was widely viewed as the next high bar to clear for the AI trade. The stock opened at US$111.50 shortly before noon. After the company’s market valuation briefly surpassed US$2 trillion, its momentum began to lose steam.
“The Anthropic IPO is attracting gobs of attention,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital in St. Louis, Missouri. “That money is coming from somewhere; investors are making changes in their portfolio to incorporate Anthropic, so I wouldn’t extrapolate a whole lot of meaning from today’s trading behaviour, whether it’s up or down.”
Even so, Ellerbroek’s enthusiasm for the AI trade has waned.
“My beliefs about the growth in data centre capex spending have come down a little bit over the last month or two,” he added. “Nvidia’s crisis situation is a big deal. The midterm elections have had an impact.”
“Data centres are going to be more expensive to build and they’re going to be built more slowly.”
Advanced Micro Devices shares tumbled after investigative outlet Hunterbrook said its affiliated fund, Hunterbrook Capital, had taken a short position in the company.
Most chipmakers were lower, including Micron and Broadcom, among others.
Nvidia marked its sixth straight session of losses after the chipmaker’s upbeat revenue forecast did little to lift sentiment.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed lower.
Neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius sustained steep losses.
In other stocks, Palo Alto Networks shares jumped after the cybersecurity firm raised its 2027 revenue guidance.
Walmart Odipped after the retail giant’s annual sales forecast disappointed investors.
According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 148.39 points, or 2.03%, to end at 7,175.24 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 544.00 points, or 2.23%, to 23,885.88. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,102.71 points, or 2.20%, to 49,095.46.
Focus turns to the Fed
Following Wednesday’s release of minutes from the US Federal Reserve’s October policy meeting, investors are recalibrating their expectations pertaining to upcoming rate decisions.
The minutes revealed a desire to rein in inflation even prior to the recent release of consumer and producer price indexes, which showed price pressures heating up.
Financial markets are currently pricing in about a 94% likelihood of a 25-basis-point rate hike at the central bank’s December meeting, with a small but growing chance of a super-sized 50-basis-point increase, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.
Next week, the Commerce Department is expected to release its personal consumption expenditures (PCE) report, which includes the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index. Analysts expect the report to show year-on-year core inflation of 3.2%, well above the central bank’s 2% annual target.

On Thursday its value briefly rose above $2 trillion, when it was launched on the Nasdaq in New York.
It is the biggest public offering ever, the first of an AI giant, and it comes with a 94-page health warning from the company itself, that includes warnings like “our products could help terrorists develop biological weapons” or “even trigger the extinction of the human race”.
It is believed between 400 and 1,000 early hires at Anthropic are now worth at least $100 million.

sources.news_title: Anthropic Makes Historic $2 Trillion Debut on Wall Street
sources.text:
Anthropic made its blockbuster Wall Street debut after an initial public offering, but it was not enough to prevent a broader market selloff.
Listed under the “ANT” ticker symbol on the Nasdaq, the Claude maker opened at $111.50 per share on Nov. 19.
The stock ended the day up 17 percent from its IPO price to finish at $97.17 a share.
Its fully diluted market cap climbed to as high as $2 trillion following its debut earlier in the session. Anthropic’s valuation was $1.27 trillion at the closing bell.
Shares were higher than Anthropic’s projected price of $70 to $78 per share in its updated prospectus released earlier this month.
Before ringing the opening bell, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei struck an optimistic tone while also offering a word of caution. While pointing to the “very real risks” of artificial intelligence (AI), he also said the goal is to make the industry better, “regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.”
“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better,” he said.
Meanwhile, the AI juggernaut allowed its underwriters the option to purchase up to 147 million extra Class A shares. If the option is fully exercised, Anthropic could raise an extra $12.2 billion, bringing its entire IPO haul to $93.5 billion.
Stocks Plunge
Anthropic ended the day in the green, but the broader stock market was swimming in a sea of red ink.
The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 1,100, or 2.19 percent, to below 49,100.

Anthropic hits $2 trillion valuation in record Nasdaq debut, surpassing Elon Musk’s SpaceX
Anthropic made Wall Street history on Thursday, November 19, 2026, reaching a staggering $2 trillion market valuation in its Nasdaq debut and surpassing Elon Musk’s SpaceX to claim the largest initial public offering on record. The milestone puts the maker of the Claude AI chatbot among the world’s most valuable companies, marking a defining moment for an artificial intelligence industry facing growing questions about its extraordinary spending.
Shares of Anthropic opened at $111.50, a 34% jump from its $83 IPO price, sending the company’s valuation past $2 trillion, according to CNBC. The early excitement faded as investors took profits, with shares retreating to around $99 during the session.
The debut comes at a delicate moment for the AI industry. After years of enthusiasm that sent technology valuations soaring, investors are beginning to question whether the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into AI infrastructure will produce returns large enough to justify the spending.
Anthropic’s listing suggests investors still see enormous potential in frontier AI. The question now is how much they’re willing to pay.
Anthropic’s record $81 billion IPO eclipses SpaceX
Anthropic raised approximately $81.3 billion through its public offering, selling 980 million shares at $83 apiece. The offering price exceeded its initial marketed range of $70 to $78, reflecting strong institutional demand ahead of the listing.
The IPO surpassed SpaceX’s record-setting June 2026 offering, giving Anthropic the distinction of completing the largest public stock offering in history.
The total fundraising package exceeds $107 billion after including a separate $26 billion private placement backed by major technology companies, including Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron and TSMC.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led the underwriting syndicate, which is expected to collect approximately $550 million in fees.
For Anthropic’s founders and early employees, the listing represents an extraordinary financial windfall. CEO Dario Amodei and his six co-founders collectively hold approximately 10% of the company, with their combined stakes valued at nearly $150 billion at the IPO price, according to Reuters.
Thousands of employees and early investors could emerge as paper millionaires, making the offering one of the largest wealth-creation events in Silicon Valley history.
Yet the excitement extends beyond Anthropic.
The company is the first major frontier AI developer to enter public markets, giving investors direct exposure to a business building advanced AI models rather than selling the chips and computing infrastructure supporting them.
Its market performance could establish a new valuation benchmark for the sector, particularly for rival OpenAI, which is expected to face similar scrutiny ahead of a potential public listing.
Wall Street’s $2 trillion bet comes with enormous risks
Anthropic’s market debut comes amid growing concerns that the AI industry’s financial ambitions may be outpacing its ability to generate sustainable profits.
The company has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet, Google’s parent company. Those obligations highlight the immense costs associated with training and operating advanced AI systems.
The scale of those commitments raises a fundamental question: Can AI companies generate enough revenue and profit to support the infrastructure they’re committing to build?
Anthropic has acknowledged that borrowing could become part of its financing strategy.
“At some point in the future we’re hoping to be investment grade, and debt is an instrument that we have available to us, and we’d like to use at some point in the future,” Amodei told CNBC.
Investors are increasingly concerned about circular financing arrangements involving AI developers, cloud providers and semiconductor companies. Such agreements can support growth across the industry, yet raise questions about how much demand comes from independent customers rather than interconnected investment relationships.
Some market strategists believe Anthropic’s strong debut says more about investors’ fear of missing the next major technology company than its near-term profitability.
“We like the enterprise AI narrative, but we do not like overpaying for market sentiment. It isn’t a prudent ‘buy-at-any-price’ opportunity for retail wealth clients,” said Talley Leger, chief market strategist at The Wealth Consulting Group, Reuters reported.
The company’s first trading session illustrated that tension. Investors initially pushed its valuation beyond $2 trillion before the stock surrendered some of its gains, reflecting uncertainty around AI valuations.
For Anthropic, the IPO has settled one question: Wall Street is prepared to commit extraordinary sums to the future of artificial intelligence.
The harder test begins after the celebrations end. Anthropic must now prove that its growing enterprise AI business can eventually generate profits commensurate with its historic valuation.
A $2 trillion debut makes Anthropic a Wall Street giant. It doesn’t guarantee the company can deliver $2 trillion worth of results.

Anthropic shares closed 17% higher in their record Nasdaq debut on Thursday (November 19, 2026), defying a broad Wall Street sell-off as investors shrugged off the Nvidia spy scandal and fears of a tech bubble to back the AI giant.
The shares ended at around $97, up from the $83 at which the company priced its shares on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), already above its expected range.
They had opened at $111.50, briefly valuing the maker of the Claude chatbot at about $2 trillion.
The gain came on a rough day for the market, with both the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the broader S&P 500 closing down more than two percent.
Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion in the offering. The IPO price valued the company at about $1.5 trillion, including employee stock options and restricted shares. At the close, it was worth about $1.75 trillion.
The debut marks a milestone in the AI boom. A company founded five years ago by OpenAI defectors worried about AI safety has become the first of the leading model developers to list on Wall Street, at a valuation rivalling decades-old tech brands.
The offering made thousands of Anthropic employees millionaires and rewarded Silicon Valley venture capitalists who backed a company that once trailed rivals OpenAI and Google.
The listing, under the ticker “ANT,” gives ordinary investors their first chance to bet directly on a stand-alone AI giant.
“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” chief executive Dario Amodei said at the Nasdaq in New York’s Times Square, underlining the company’s priority of promoting safe AI.
The offering surpasses the $75 billion that Elon Musk’s SpaceX raised in its June IPO at a valuation of $1.77 trillion.
‘Breath of fresh air’
SpaceX’s total ultimately rose to $86 billion after its underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares. Anthropic has granted its underwriters a similar option, which would lift its total to about $93.5 billion.
“This may be the breath of fresh air that the tech trade needed to move beyond the fog of artificial intelligence that we’ve been living in for the last couple of weeks,” Art Hogan of B. Riley Wealth Management told AFP.
The strong demand comes even as AI stocks have swung sharply, with investors questioning whether heavy spending on the technology will pay off.
Nvidia, the chip giant at the centre of the AI investment boom and an investor in Anthropic and dozens of other AI companies, has been shaken by the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang after a reported affair with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy.
Anthropic’s Claude models are among the most powerful in the world, hailed for their problem-solving potential but also feared for their capacity to destabilise societies and replace human workers.
The five-year-old company’s revenue has surged at a pace few U.S. companies have ever matched, reaching $17 billion in the third quarter, up from $1.4 billion a year earlier.
Much of that revenue comes from customers paying to use its AI models for computer coding. Its massive computing costs remain a major question for investors.
Anthropic has disclosed about $900 billion in commitments for computing capacity and warned in its filing that it must make many of those payments even if demand falls short.
‘One stop’
Mr. Amodei and his sister Daniela, the company’s president, founded Anthropic with several colleagues in 2021 after leaving ChatGPT-maker OpenAI.
Daniela Amodei told CNBC the listing was only “one stop on the journey” for the company.
“We’re going to wake up tomorrow and we’re going to be the same company,” she said.
Anthropic’s IPO filing went into extensive detail on the risks of AI technology, reflecting the company’s focus on safety even as it builds ever more powerful models.
It warns that advanced AI systems “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.”
Critics accuse the company of using its safety message as cover while releasing powerful technology, casting itself as the responsible steward of an industry it is racing to lead.
“The company uses safety branding to court investors, employees, and the public — even as it has quietly weakened its safety pledges and lobbied for self-serving regulation,” said a public statement, titled Misanthropic, signed by prominent academics.

sources.news_title: What to know about Anthropic’s massive IPO as it breaks records on Wall Street – WTOP News
sources.text:
A little-known Silicon Valley startup just a few years ago, Anthropic, the maker of the popular Claude chatbot, went public in a record-setting stock listing.
As it has grown into a giant in the booming artificial intelligence industry, Anthropic has also sprinted ahead of rival OpenAI in the race to sell shares to investors. At the start of trading Thursday, Anthropic’s valuation leaped to $2.01 trillion, surpassing SpaceX as the largest IPO on record.
Here is what to know about the initial public offering.
Anthropic is going public despite a jittery market
It’s not the most ideal time for an artificial intelligence company to sell stock. While tech stocks have done well so far this year, some AI-related stocks, notably data center companies, have seen stomach-churning price movements in recent weeks.
Adding to the sector volatility has been the turmoil at Nvidia, the chipmaker that’s been a linchpin of the AI industry. CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation following reports of extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, has weighed heavily on the company’s stock, and dragged the broader S&P 500 down.
Meanwhile, there are question marks over Anthropic’s finances because borrowing costs are rising. That matters because the company, which is unprofitable and already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, has a voracious need for cash to build more computing and infrastructure to power its growth.
The company could face tougher regulatory pressure from newly elected Democrats who have vowed to crack down on data center construction.
But on the plus side, by beating OpenAI to the market, Anthropic could get an important advantage should investors suddenly fear they have too much exposure to the sector and decide they don’t want to buy stock in the next public AI company.
The company promises to pursue the public’s benefit – as well as profits
The new pressure to deliver profits for shareholders will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence.
Like rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good.
In regulatory filings, the company has sketched out a governance structure to protect the company’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests.
The company has set up a long-term benefit trust that will be able to elect or remove a majority of the company’s board of directors. This trust will not run day-to-day operations but its influence means the company could opt for strategies that might not make the most money for investors in the long term.
Still, the structure gives the company wide leeway to decide how to measure whether it’s benefiting society, experts say.
“I think then the real test emerges if and when the question of public benefit becomes costly” — or when the public benefit comes into conflict with making a profit, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute.
There’s a lot for investors to consider
Anthropic’s initial public offering will be a big test not only for the company itself but also for the entire artificial-intelligence industry and the U.S. stock market itself.
It will likely affect even people who make no changes to their 401(k) accounts.
Anthropic’s market value could exceed that of Meta Platforms, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, and make it more valuable than Coca-Cola, IBM, Starbucks, Delta Air Lines and General Motors — combined.
At that size, Anthropic could quickly join indexes that track wide swaths of the stock market, which in turn could bring in even more investment.
The company expects up to 20% of its Class A shares in the IPO to go to what are called “retail investors.”
But as part of the IPO, Anthropic is creating a special class of stock for CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, giving them 50.1% of the voting power of all the company’s outstanding shares.
That means the founders as a group could overshadow every other shareholder and dictate issues put before all investors, like how to vote on a potential sale of the company.

That’s the index’s longest losing streak since 2024, and it’s down 8.2 per cent from its record set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 2.2 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite sank 2.3 per cent. The losses were widespread, and more than 90 per cent of the stocks that make up the S&P 500 fell.
Leading them downward was Williams-Sonoma, which dropped 15.2 per cent after the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm reported revenue for the latest quarter that was just below Wall Street’s forecast. It also stuck with its forecast for how much revenue it will make throughout 2026, and the midpoint of that range was below what analysts were expecting.
Walmart sank 1 per cent even though it reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations.
Earlier in the morning, AI-related stocks seemed to be doing well enough to more than make up for such losses.
They had rallied after Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sold its stock at a price of $US83 each in its initial public offering. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund the industry’s growth. Then came this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterm elections, which raised concerns about more regulation for AI.
Most recently, it was the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. He had been one of AI’s biggest evangelists and helped build interest in the industry while also using some of Nvidia’s massive profits to further fund its growth.

Perpetual futures, contracts that track a price with no expiry date and settle in crypto rather than shares, let traders bet on ANT before it listed. sources.news_title: What to know about Anthropic’s massive IPO as it breaks records on Wall Street
sources.text:
By The Associated Press
A little-known Silicon Valley startup just a few years ago, Anthropic, the maker of the popular Claude chatbot, went public in a record-setting stock listing.
As it has grown into a giant in the booming artificial intelligence industry, Anthropic has also sprinted ahead of rival OpenAI in the race to sell shares to investors. At the start of trading Thursday, Anthropic’s valuation leaped to $2.01 trillion, surpassing SpaceX as the largest IPO on record.
Here is what to know about the initial public offering.
Anthropic is going public despite a jittery market
It’s not the most ideal time for an artificial intelligence company to sell stock. While tech stocks have done well so far this year, some AI-related stocks, notably data center companies, have seen stomach-churning price movements in recent weeks.
Adding to the sector volatility has been the turmoil at Nvidia, the chipmaker that’s been a linchpin of the AI industry. CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation following reports of extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, has weighed heavily on the company’s stock, and dragged the broader S&P 500 down.
Meanwhile, there are question marks over Anthropic’s finances because borrowing costs are rising. That matters because the company, which is unprofitable and already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, has a voracious need for cash to build more computing and infrastructure to power its growth.
The company could face tougher regulatory pressure from newly elected Democrats who have vowed to crack down on data center construction.
But on the plus side, by beating OpenAI to the market, Anthropic could get an important advantage should investors suddenly fear they have too much exposure to the sector and decide they don’t want to buy stock in the next public AI company.
The company promises to pursue the public’s benefit – as well as profits
The new pressure to deliver profits for shareholders will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence.
Like rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good.
In regulatory filings, the company has sketched out a governance structure to protect the company’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests.
The company has set up a long-term benefit trust that will be able to elect or remove a majority of the company’s board of directors. This trust will not run day-to-day operations but its influence means the company could opt for strategies that might not make the most money for investors in the long term.
Still, the structure gives the company wide leeway to decide how to measure whether it’s benefiting society, experts say.
“I think then the real test emerges if and when the question of public benefit becomes costly” — or when the public benefit comes into conflict with making a profit, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute.
There’s a lot for investors to consider
Anthropic’s initial public offering will be a big test not only for the company itself but also for the entire artificial-intelligence industry and the U.S. stock market itself.
It will likely affect even people who make no changes to their 401(k) accounts.
Anthropic’s market value could exceed that of Meta Platforms, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, and make it more valuable than Coca-Cola, IBM, Starbucks, Delta Air Lines and General Motors — combined.
At that size, Anthropic could quickly join indexes that track wide swaths of the stock market, which in turn could bring in even more investment.
The company expects up to 20% of its Class A shares in the IPO to go to what are called “retail investors.”
But as part of the IPO, Anthropic is creating a special class of stock for CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, giving them 50.1% of the voting power of all the company’s outstanding shares.
That means the founders as a group could overshadow every other shareholder and dictate issues put before all investors, like how to vote on a potential sale of the company.

sources.news_title: Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut
sources.text:
Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.
Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.
For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.
But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.
Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.
A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.
The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.
Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.
“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.
In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”
Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.
What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.
OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.
Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.
Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

What to know about Anthropic's massive IPO as it breaks records on Wall Street
A little-known Silicon Valley startup just a few years ago, Anthropic, the maker of the popular Claude chatbot, went public in a record-setting stock listing.
As it has grown into a giant in the booming artificial intelligence industry, Anthropic has also sprinted ahead of rival OpenAI in the race to sell shares to investors. At the start of trading Thursday, Anthropic's valuation leaped to $2.01 trillion, surpassing SpaceX as the largest IPO on record.
Here is what to know about the initial public offering.
Anthropic is going public despite a jittery market
It’s not the most ideal time for an artificial intelligence company to sell stock. While tech stocks have done well so far this year, some AI-related stocks, notably data center companies, have seen stomach-churning price movements in recent weeks.
Adding to the sector volatility has been the turmoil at Nvidia, the chipmaker that's been a linchpin of the AI industry. CEO Jensen Huang's resignation following reports of extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, has weighed heavily on the company's stock, and dragged the broader S&P 500 down.
Meanwhile, there are question marks over Anthropic's finances because borrowing costs are rising. That matters because the company, which is unprofitable and already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, has a voracious need for cash to build more computing and infrastructure to power its growth.
The company could face tougher regulatory pressure from newly elected Democrats who have vowed to crack down on data center construction.
But on the plus side, by beating OpenAI to the market, Anthropic could get an important advantage should investors suddenly fear they have too much exposure to the sector and decide they don’t want to buy stock in the next public AI company.
The company promises to pursue the public’s benefit – as well as profits
The new pressure to deliver profits for shareholders will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence.
Like rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good.
In regulatory filings, the company has sketched out a governance structure to protect the company’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests.
The company has set up a long-term benefit trust that will be able to elect or remove a majority of the company’s board of directors. This trust will not run day-to-day operations but its influence means the company could opt for strategies that might not make the most money for investors in the long term.
Still, the structure gives the company wide leeway to decide how to measure whether it’s benefiting society, experts say.
“I think then the real test emerges if and when the question of public benefit becomes costly” — or when the public benefit comes into conflict with making a profit, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute.
There’s a lot for investors to consider
Anthropic’s initial public offering will be a big test not only for the company itself but also for the entire artificial-intelligence industry and the U.S. stock market itself.
It will likely affect even people who make no changes to their 401(k) accounts.
Anthropic’s market value could exceed that of Meta Platforms, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, and make it more valuable than Coca-Cola, IBM, Starbucks, Delta Air Lines and General Motors — combined.
At that size, Anthropic could quickly join indexes that track wide swaths of the stock market, which in turn could bring in even more investment.
The company expects up to 20% of its Class A shares in the IPO to go to what are called “retail investors.”
But as part of the IPO, Anthropic is creating a special class of stock for CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, giving them 50.1% of the voting power of all the company’s outstanding shares.
That means the founders as a group could overshadow every other shareholder and dictate issues put before all investors, like how to vote on a potential sale of the company.

Anthropic soars 34% to US$2 trillion valuation on Wall Street debut
- Anthropic rose more than 34% in its Nasdaq debut, valuing the AI firm at about US$2 trillion and making it the first major model maker to list on Wall Street.
- The IPO raised a record US$81.3 billion, with strong demand despite AI stock swings, the Nvidia spy scandal, and fears of a tech bubble.
- CEO Dario Amodei said the listing strengthens the company’s finances and safety mission, while critics warned advanced AI could bring “catastrophic or existential risks”.
AI generated
NEW YORK - Anthropic shares soared more than 34% in their Nasdaq debut on Nov 19, pushing the AI giant’s value to about US$2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion) as investors shrugged off the Nvidia spy scandal and fears of a tech bubble.
The shares opened at US$111.50, up from the US$83 at which the company priced its shares on Nov 18, already above its expected range.
Anthropic raised a record US$81.3 billion, selling 980 million shares, about 956 million of them new shares and the rest from existing shareholders. The company itself will receive about US$79.4 billion.
The IPO’s original price valued the maker of the Claude chatbot at about US$1.5 trillion, including employee stock options and restricted shares.
The roughly US$2 trillion valuation at the open matches estimates floated earlier this year, before AI stocks slid on Wall Street.
The debut marks a milestone in the AI boom. A company founded five years ago by OpenAI defectors worried about AI safety has become the first of the leading model developers to list on Wall Street, at a valuation rivalling decades-old tech brands.
The listing, under the ticker “ANT,” gives ordinary investors their first chance to bet directly on a stand-alone AI giant.
“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” chief executive Dario Amodei said at the Nasdaq in New York’s Times Square, underlining the company’s priority of promoting safe AI.
‘Fresh air’
As is usual for large listings, the shares began trading well after the opening bell, once Nasdaq and the lead investment banks had gathered buy and sell orders to set an opening price.
The offering surpasses the US$75 billion that Elon Musk’s SpaceX raised in its June IPO at a valuation of US$1.77 trillion.
SpaceX’s total ultimately rose to US$86 billion after its underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares. SpaceX shares opened 11% above their IPO price.
Anthropic has granted its underwriters an option to buy up to 147 million more shares, which would lift its total to about US$93.5 billion.
“Demand seems to be outstripping supply of this newly publicly traded company,” Art Hogan of B. Riley Wealth Management told AFP.
“This may be the breath of fresh air that the tech trade needed to move beyond the fog of artificial intelligence that we’ve been living in for the last couple of weeks,” he added.
The strong demand comes even as AI stocks have swung sharply, with investors questioning whether heavy spending on the technology will pay off.
Nvidia, the chip giant at the centre of the AI investment boom and an investor in Anthropic and dozens of other AI companies, has been shaken by the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang after a reported affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy.
Anthropic’s Claude models are among the most powerful in the world, hailed for their problem-solving potential but also feared for their capacity to destabilise societies and replace human workers.
The five-year-old company’s revenue has surged at a pace few US companies have ever matched, reaching US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from US$1.4 billion a year earlier.
Much of that revenue comes from customers paying to use its AI models for computer coding.
Amodei and his sister Daniela, the company’s president, founded Anthropic with several colleagues in 2021 after leaving ChatGPT-maker OpenAI.
Threats to Americans
Anthropic’s IPO filing goes into extensive detail on the risks of the technology, reflecting the company’s focus on safety even as it builds ever more powerful models.
It warns that advanced AI systems “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.”
US Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren criticised the listing on X, saying the company “fails to answer for the potential threats to Americans’ retirements and the entire financial system if this IPO goes awry.”
About a dozen protesters gathered outside the Nasdaq on Nov 19, chanting: “Why you doing IPO? This AI bubble’s about to blow!” AFP

Nov. 19 — Anthropic’s market value climbed as high as $2.1 trillion during its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, surpassing SpaceX’s massive June listing as investors rushed to buy shares of the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot.
Shares opened at $111.50, approximately 34% above the initial public offering price of $83. The stock was last trading at $105.11, marking a blockbuster debut for the world’s first publicly traded frontier AI company.
The strong performance comes after a turbulent period for the technology sector, including the departure of Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang and growing concerns about the enormous costs associated with developing and expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Anthropic’s successful listing offers renewed encouragement to an AI industry that has faced increasing investor skepticism in recent weeks.
“I’ve looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI. Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies,” said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, ahead of the debut.
Anthropic Becomes a New Benchmark for AI Companies
Anthropic’s public-market debut is expected to establish an important valuation benchmark for the frontier AI industry, particularly as rival OpenAI reportedly considers going public in 2027.
The company sold 980 million shares at $83 each, pricing its IPO above the initial range of $70 to $78 established when it began its investor roadshow.
Proceeds from the offering could reach as much as $93.5 billion if underwriters exercise their option to purchase additional shares in full.
Including an additional $26 billion raised through a private placement, the total figure exceeds $107 billion.
The private placement attracted investments from major technology and semiconductor companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google parent Alphabet, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company.
The blockbuster offering also represents a significant payday for its underwriters. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the underwriting group, which is set to receive a combined $550 million fee, according to a regulatory filing.
Anthropic has now joined the trillion-dollar group alongside established technology giants such as Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia.
Founders Stand to Gain Nearly $150 Billion
The IPO is expected to create substantial wealth for Anthropic’s founders, employees and early contributors.
Based on the offering price, CEO Dario Amodei and the company’s six other co-founders collectively hold approximately 10% of Anthropic, giving their combined stakes an estimated value of nearly $150 billion, according to calculations based on regulatory disclosures.
The listing is also expected to create thousands of paper millionaires, extending the financial rewards beyond the company’s leadership to researchers, engineers and administrative employees.
However, the stock’s performance in the days following its debut will determine how much of that wealth remains reflected in their holdings.
Investors Weigh AI Growth Against Mounting Costs
Despite the extraordinary market reception, questions remain about whether Anthropic can justify its valuation over the long term.
The broader AI industry faces increasing scrutiny over the scale of investment required to develop advanced models, secure computing capacity and expand data center infrastructure.
Anthropic has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners that include Amazon and Google’s Alphabet, highlighting its dependence on securing enormous amounts of future computing resources.
These commitments also raise questions about financing, profitability and the sustainability of the company’s expansion.
CEO Dario Amodei indicated that Anthropic may eventually turn to debt markets to support its operations.
“At some point in the future we’re hoping to be investment grade, and debt is an instrument that we have available to us, and we’d like to use at some point in the future,” Amodei told CNBC.
Some investors remain unconvinced that the company’s growth trajectory will translate into sustainable profits.
“Anthropic is a one-trick pony. People compare it with Amazon because even Amazon lost money for several years, but Anthropic won’t have that luxury,” said Bill Gunderson, partner at GCG Advisory Partners.
“They’ve got to get to profitability soon.”
A Critical Test for the Future of Artificial Intelligence
Anthropic’s debut arrives amid an intensifying debate over whether the AI boom is approaching bubble territory.
Much of the concern centers on interconnected financing arrangements among AI developers, semiconductor manufacturers, cloud providers and investors. Critics question whether some of the industry’s rapid growth is being supported by money circulating within the same network rather than by independently generated demand.
Anthropic’s strong debut suggests that investor appetite for leading AI companies remains substantial, even as technology stocks experience broader volatility.
However, the company must demonstrate that its growth can support its enormous computing commitments and justify its valuation.
There are also broader concerns about the pace of AI development. In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic warned that artificial intelligence systems could behave unpredictably and advance faster than the mechanisms designed to oversee them.
The company’s public-market performance will therefore be watched closely as a potential indicator of investor confidence in the next generation of AI businesses.
With OpenAI reportedly considering a 2027 listing, Anthropic’s debut may become the reference point against which future AI offerings are measured.

“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
The company’s rival, OpenAI, is not planning to go public until next year.
IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt
Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.
While the company has ample cash for now, it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.
An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That’s partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability.
Anthropic’s IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei.
The offering consists of 980 million shares of Class A common stock, 956.3 million of which are being sold by Anthropic and 23.6 million of which are being sold by certain stockholders.
AI industry faces concerns about data centers, a possible bubble and regulations
Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business.
Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.
Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months.
Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction.
Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group.
“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & the World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.”

sources.text:
Anthropic begins public trading in major test for promise and risk of AI
Anthropic opened at a price of $111.50 a share.
By Max Zahn
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday at a price of $111.50 a share.
The company behind popular chatbot Claude immediately vaulted into rarefied air among some of the largest public companies in the world.
The share price at the open of trading came in more than 30% higher than an offer price of $83 a share, which had valued the company at about $1.5 trillion.
The IPO arrived at a tumultuous moment for the AI industry, however.
Public concern over potential catastrophic risks posed by AI has grown in recent months, resulting in part from security incidents disclosed by Anthropic as well as the high-profile resignation of a researcher at the company.
Nvidia, a high-flying AI firm and a partner of Anthropic, suffered a leadership shakeup last week as CEO Jensen Huang stepped down over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down about 4% since Huang resigned.
Huang admitted in an internal message to Nvidia staff that he had been "unfaithful to his wife," though he did not name the person with whom he had been involved.
Here's what to know about the Anthropic IPO:
Why did Anthropic move forward with an IPO?
The IPO pulled in fresh funds for the San Francisco-based firm, which aims to compete in a potentially lucrative but cost-intensive section of the AI industry centered on advanced models and the tools they empower.
"Building and scaling frontier intelligence is one of the most important and capital-intensive endeavors in history," Anthropic said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
Anthropic priced its initial public offering of 980 million shares at $83 a share -- raising $81 billion. Anthropic traded under the ticker symbol "ANT."
The company significantly expanded its revenue at the outset of 2026, but it continued to suffer losses.
Anthropic earned $16.3 billion in revenue over the first six months of this year, growing nearly 14-fold from the same period a year earlier, according to a government filing.
Still, the company reported a net loss of $80.7 billion over the first six months of this year, indicating the scale of its spending over that period.
Did the Anthropic IPO make the company's founders billionaires?
Anthropic boasts seven co-founders, and each of them was expected to become a multi-billionaire after the company went public.
The most well-known co-founder is CEO Dario Amodei, who has drawn attention for repeated warnings about the risks posed by AI.
The company's other founders are Daniela Amodei, the company's chair, president and Dario's sister; Tom Brown, chief compute officer; Jack Clark, head of public benefit; Jared Kaplan, chief science officer; Sam McCandlish, chief architect; and Christopher Olah, interpretability research lead.
The founders each hold a stake of 3.6% to 3.7% of the company's voting common shares, and they each planned to sell a small portion of their stake when the company went public, according to a financial filing.
At the previously anticipated share price of $70 to $78, the portion of the stake to be sold by each one would have amounted to about $250 million. The remaining stake held by each -- about 3.2% -- would have been valued at more than $17 billion.
Will Anthropic stock be in your 401(k)?
Anthropic will all but certainly become a part of people's 401(k) accounts soon. Those accounts often hold index funds, which are pegged to major indexes like the Nasdaq.
Until recently, newly listed companies were barred from major indexes until after an extended waiting period. But the Nasdaq issued a rule change in May permitting "fast entry" to the Nasdaq-100 for some major IPOs. Over the ensuing weeks, some other top exchanges also tweaked their rules, though their eligibility requirements vary.
"Although Anthropic is unlikely to join the S&P 500 before late 2027 because of eligibility requirements, it is expected to be added to other indexes relatively soon after listing," Brian Therien, senior analyst at Edward Jones, told ABC News in a statement.
As such, it won't take long for Anthropic to become a part of 401(k) holdings.
What do analysts think of the stock?
In the run-up to its IPO, Anthropic touted AI as a transformational and lucrative technology, while warning about possible catastrophic risk that could bring financial fallout for shareholders.
A financial filing last month presents AI as "one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort."
In the same document, Anthropic warned of the possibility its AI models could pose a "catastrophic or existential risk to humanity."
Investing in the company's stock "involves a high degree of risk," Anthropic added.
In a report ahead of the IPO, financial research firm Morningstar voiced optimism about the stock but also cautioned about a very high degree of uncertainty surrounding the firm's prospects.
"We have a positive outlook on Anthropic's ability to remain at the frontier of artificial intelligence model research," Morningstar said, adding that the company could monetize such research by "selling primarily to enterprise customers."
Still, Morningstar said its warning about uncertainty "reflects our view on the wide range of financial outcomes for a business investing heavily in large language models, a nascent technology."

Summary
Anthropic reached a valuation of about $2 trillion in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, surpassing SpaceX’s June listing as investors weighed the AI sector’s prospects. Shares opened at $111.5, 34 percent above the $83 IPO price, before falling to around $99. The listing made Anthropic the first publicly traded frontier AI company and is expected to make its stock a benchmark for the sector. Investors remain concerned about the cost of AI infrastructure and whether future returns will justify it.
Key Facts
- Anthropic sold 980 million shares at $83 each, above its initial price range of $70 to $78.
- IPO proceeds could reach $93.5 billion if underwriters exercise their option to buy additional shares; the total raised, including a $26 billion private placement, is over $107 billion.
- AMD, Broadcom, Alphabet’s Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC invested in the private placement.
- Anthropic has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet’s Google.

Anthropic notched a valuation of about $2 trillion in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, vaulting past SpaceX's massive June listing and capping a turbulent stretch for the AI sector that tested Wall Street's appetite for the technology.
The early exuberance, however, partly faded, signaling volatility ahead as investors locked in quick gains and the main indexes retreated amid renewed jitters over the sector's outlook.

AI technology has boosted economic growth, but sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-center-skeptic Democratic tsunami in the US midterm elections.
Investors who once embraced the boom have turned skeptical in recent weeks over concerns that the enormous spending needed to build out the sector and the mounting debt loads may not be justified by the eventual returns.
Anthropic, too, has signaled it may tap debt markets.

An industry benchmark
As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark. The company sold 980 million shares at $83 each, pricing the IPO above its initial range of $70 to $78 set when it launched the road show.

Anthropic's IPO is set to create thousands of paper millionaires and a handful of billionaires.

Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, CEOs and political leaders split over its sustainability.

Anthropic has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, underscoring how its rapid growth hinges on securing vast amounts of future computing capacity, some of which relies on financing beyond the company's control.
Investors will be watching Anthropic's debut and subsequent trading closely, with analysts expecting the stock to emerge as a proxy for the broader AI trade.

READ MORE: Anthropic prices its IPO at $83 per share, valuing the AI giant at $1.5 trillion Its shares shot higher as trading began and held on to much of those gains to close up 17% at $97.17. The initial offering overtook SpaceX as the largest IPO in history. Anthropic's initial offer of $82 per share was surprisingly high given the investor worries that ratcheted up even more recently following the stunning ouster of AI's chief promoter, the CEO of Nvidia, in a possible Chinese spying scandal. Anthropic had earlier set a lower price range between $70 and $78 per share. Stand with free and independent journalism. Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited. Adding to the pressure to go public was the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently. Market valuation for AI companies is going to be "up and down for many years to come, but more up than down," said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group. sources.text:
Anthropic Stock Surges 34% In Nasdaq Debut. AI Giant Hits $2.1 Trillion Valuation.
Claude maker Anthropic opened at $111.50, well above its $83 IPO price, as Wall Street rushed into the record-breaking AI listing.
Anthropic shares surged 34% in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday, opening at $111.50 against their $83 initial public offering price and briefly pushing the Claude developer's market valuation to $2.1 trillion.
The opening price surpassed earlier indications of approximately $105, marking a stronger-than-expected debut for the artificial intelligence company behind Claude. The stock subsequently retreated from its opening level, trading at $105.11 in a Thursday market update, as investors weighed the extraordinary valuation against the company's rapidly growing revenue and substantial computing costs.
The $2.1 trillion peak placed Anthropic among the world's most valuable publicly traded companies and surpassed the valuation achieved during SpaceX's stock market debut in June.
The listing also marks the first time investors have been able to buy shares in a publicly traded developer of frontier AI models, offering direct exposure to a company competing with OpenAI and Google in the race to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems.
Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT after completing the largest initial public offering on record.
The company's official pricing announcement confirmed Wednesday that it sold 980 million shares at $83 each, giving the public offering a gross value of approximately $81.34 billion.
Anthropic itself sold roughly 956.4 million shares, while existing stockholders offered another 23.6 million. The company will not receive proceeds from shares sold by those stockholders.
The IPO price exceeded the company's previously proposed range of $70 to $78 per share, reflecting strong investor demand even before the shares began trading.
For investors allocated shares at $83, the $111.50 opening price represented a paper gain of $28.50 per share, or approximately 34.3%, before fees.
However, investors purchasing shares at the opening price would not receive that same return. The subsequent retreat to $105.11 illustrated how quickly prices can fluctuate during a highly anticipated stock market debut.
At that level, Anthropic shares remained approximately 26.6% above their IPO price, although the figure represented a reported intraday trading level rather than a final closing price.
The debut comes at a sensitive moment for the wider AI market.
Technology stocks have faced renewed scrutiny over the extraordinary amounts being spent on computing infrastructure, with investors questioning whether rapid growth in artificial intelligence revenue will ultimately justify the cost of developing and operating advanced models.
Anthropic's success in attracting public investors suggests that demand for leading AI companies remains strong despite those concerns.
Yet the company's valuation places enormous expectations on its ability to turn revenue growth into sustainable profits.
Anthropic reported approximately $33.2 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026, according to its IPO prospectus filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
That expansion has been accompanied by substantial spending on the computing resources required to train and operate increasingly powerful AI models.
The company has also entered into major computing commitments with technology partners, including Amazon and Google's parent company, Alphabet, highlighting the scale of infrastructure investment needed to maintain its position in the industry.
While its revenue has expanded rapidly, Anthropic remains unprofitable on a cumulative basis, leaving investors to assess how soon the business can generate sustained earnings and cash flow.
The debut may also influence expectations surrounding other major artificial intelligence developers considering public listings.
OpenAI has not announced a firm IPO date, although the ChatGPT developer has indicated that becoming a publicly traded company is part of its longer-term plans.

Anthropic shares began trading at $111.50 on the company’s market debut Thursday, up 34% from its offering price.
The strong demand indicated a hearty appetite the artificial intelligence trade. Anthropic officially priced its highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO) at $83 per share. Shares officially began trading just before noon on Thursday and have fluctuated from gains between 15% and 35%.
First day pops and pullbacks are common in early trading days as the market determines the fair value for the stock. In its first two days trading, SpaceX posted double-digit gains and then on its sixth day trading, posted a double-digit loss.
Anthropic revealed on Wednesday that the company and other stockholders would be selling 980 million shares, bringing in $81.3 billion. The company trades under the ticker “ANT” and debuted at an over $2 trillion valuation, making it the largest IPO in history surpassing SpaceX, which debuted at $1.77 trillion valuation in June.
Anthropic is one of the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies, and its CEO, Dario Amodei, told investors at the company’s roadshow earlier this year that he thinks his company could create a “new age of miracles.”
“I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia,” Amodei said. “We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time.”
The company was originally planning to IPO in November which turned out to be a tumultuous month for the industry after Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang was ousted from his company after multiple affairs, including an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
AI companies also watched as their stocks fall following the 2026 midterm elections after Democrats swept the country with wins, and many Democrats promised to block data center construction.
Amodei has also called for regulations for the industry, releasing an alarming letter in September that spelled doom for the industry. The letter was titled, “We Must Pace the Frontier.” Three days before Amodei published his letter, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from the company and warned, “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic’s Alignment Science Lead Evan Hubinger said, “Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is greater than 10% within the next decade.”
Amodei said in an interview a couple days later, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”
He added, “if we take the right paths, then the chance of something going wrong is very low. If we take the wrong path, then the chance of something going wrong could be could be even higher than that. And so, let’s focus on our agency and our ability to take the right paths instead of the wrong paths.”
Former White House AI czar David Sacks questioned how the company could go public following its doomsday warnings.
“I don’t see how they can IPO now in the trillions,” he said. “How can they be allowed to IPO at this point in time?”
Tech Titan Elon Musk also joked about Anthropic’s IPO.
“There’s a 10% chance of annihilating humanity — but, by the way, how much allocation would you like in our IPO?” he said.
