Evan LeFlore, director of AI, innovation, and economic opportunity at Better Markets, noted that "anyone holding a broad index fund will likely own this company within weeks of its listing, whether or not they ever decide to buy a single share."
"They deserve to know what they are being handed," said LeFlore. "The money in this industry is moving in a circle, and every American has a stake in understanding that. The companies that sell Anthropic its computing power are also buying its stock, and Anthropic spends that money straight back with them. Each lap around the circle gets booked as revenue and treated as proof that the demand is real. This reaches well beyond the people who buy shares."
"A broad index fund already holds the suppliers on the other side of these deals, so millions of Americans are on every side of this circle without having chosen any of it, and the build-out driving it is financed substantially with debt," LeFlore added. "If the demand turns out to be thinner than the revenue suggests, the losses will not stay inside the AI industry.”
A recent report authored by experts at the Open Markets Institute and the Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund warned that the AI boom "represents one of the largest speculative frenzies in history."

"The company uses safety branding to court investors, employees, and the public—even as it has quietly weakened its safety pledges and lobbied for self-serving regulation," the statement reads. "Anthropic is not a safe AI company, and we must reject its reckless attempt to amass power in the name of the greater good."
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is running to lead the Senate Democratic caucus in the new Congress, said Wednesday that Anthropic's IPO highlights "how AI’s rapid development is great for the billionaire class but extremely dangerous for humanity."
"We need to act now to address these risks, hold AI companies accountable, and protect the American people," the senator said.

Amid mounting fears, the regulatory environment could change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry as a backlash unfolds against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors who have vowed to stop new construction.
In his comments Thursday, Amodei also touted a range of positive uses for AI, noting that Claude already is helping scientists do quicker research and that the technology could help accelerate that progress in the future.
“Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox and polio history for most of the world," he said, "but progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families."
He also pointed to Claude's use across companies, nonprofits and government services. “I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future,” he said.
Adding to the pressure to go public was the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group.
“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said Tuesday in an interview with The Associated Press at the Semafor Silicon Valley & the World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.”
___
Ortutay reported from Oakland, California. Associated Press business writers Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Michelle Chapman in New York contributed.

sources.news_title: Anthropic on course to break $2 trillion barrier
sources.text:
Anthropic was on course to hit $2 trillion in market value as its shares looked set to soar in their Nasdaq debut today, with investors rushing to own a stake in the world's first publicly traded frontier AI company.
The stock was set to open at $110.5, 33% higher than the IPO price of $83, according to indications as this afternoon.
The Claude chatbot maker's IPO, together with Tuesday's earnings report by AI poster child Nvidia, signals the industry has nominally passed the two big tests facing it this week.
Strong demand for Anthropic shares amid a broader tech selloff offers hope to a sector where euphoria has somewhat cooled in recent weeks.
"I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI. Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies," Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said before the Anthropic debut.
AI technology has boosted economic growth, sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-center-skeptic Democratic tsunami in the US midterm elections.
Investors who once embraced the boom have turned skeptical in recent weeks over concerns that the enormous spending needed to build out the sector and the mounting debt loads may not be justified by the eventual returns.
Anthropic, too, has signaled it may tap debt markets.
"At some point in the future we're hoping to be investment grade, and debt is an instrument that we have available to us, and we'd like to use at some point in the future," CEO Dario Amodei told CNBC in an interview.
An industry benchmark
As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark, with its arch-rival OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 listing.
The company sold 980 million shares at $83 each, pricing the IPO above its initial range of $70 to $78 set when it launched the road show. Its IPO proceeds could climb to as much as $93.5 billion if underwriters fully exercise their option to purchase additional shares.
Currently, the figure sits at over $107 billion, including the additional $26 billion raised through a private placement. AMD, Broadcom, Alphabet's Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC were the investors in the private placement.
"Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain," IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer said.
London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates passive demand from index-tracking funds will account for purchase of up to 30% of Anthropic's shares offered by the end of the year.
Anthropic will also join the trillion-dollar club stacked with behemoths such as Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia.
The blockbuster deal is going to earn the underwriters, led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, a $550m fee, a regulatory filing showed.
Big payday for Co-founders
Although shares can be volatile in the days following a listing, Anthropic's IPO is set to create thousands of paper millionaires and a handful of billionaires.
Based on the IPO price, CEO Amodei and his six co-founders, who together own about 10% of the company, had stakes valued at nearly $150 billion, according to a Reuters calculation based on details in the filing.
More broadly, the listing is expected to create a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff.
Justifying the price tag
Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, CEOs and political leaders split over its sustainability.
Much of the scrutiny has focused on circular financing arrangements. A complicated web of deals between AI companies, chipmakers, cloud providers and investors has raised questions over how much of the industry's growth is being fueled by money circulating within the same ecosystem.
Anthropic's breakneck growth has so far defied these concerns, but some investors have said they may wait for the initial euphoria to subside before buying.
"Anthropic is a one-trick pony. People compare it with Amazon because even Amazon lost money for several years, but Anthropic won't have that luxury," said Bill Gunderson, partner at GCG Advisory Partners.
"They've got to get to profitability soon."
Anthropic has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, underscoring how its rapid growth hinges on securing vast amounts of future computing capacity, some of which relies on financing beyond the company's control.
Investors will be watching Anthropic's debut and subsequent trading closely, with analysts expecting the stock to emerge as a proxy for the broader AI trade.
The company will also need to balance growth with calls to slow the development of advanced AI models. Anthropic warned in its IPO prospectus that AI could behave unpredictably and advance faster than oversight mechanisms.

sources.news_title: Anthropic begins trading in the biggest IPO on record despite the many fears surrounding AI
Anthropic hits $2 trillion in Nasdaq debut, tops SpaceX's June listing
This Anthropic proxy play is getting traders' attention – here's where they see it going
sources.text:
Who says you can't tailgate an IPO?
Traders are preparing for this week's blockbuster Anthropic IPO in different ways, including buying options on one publicly-traded fund that invests in private assets.
The Destiny Tech100 (DXYZ) is a publicly-traded, closed-end fund that invests in equity, equity-linked instruments, or shares of private funds and venture companies to gain exposure to private companies. Currently, 14% of the fund's assets are tied to Anthropic, according to the company's website.
Options volume on the fund jumped to more than 10x the 30-day average Monday, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Of the 42,300 contracts traded by midday, 41,800 were calls, with just 141 puts likely opened by buyers.
Just shy of $5.5 million in options premium on DXYZ traded on Monday, with almost all of it tied to calls, but just marginally more spent buying than selling calls, according to SpotGamma. The highest-volume contract is currently the 30-strike call expiring Friday, a 90-cent contract that needs the fund to rally 19% into the weekend to pay off.
Traders may want to be wary of how the fund traded around the SpaceX IPO: DXYZ surged almost 150% in May before unwinding all the gains in the weeks ahead of SpaceX's debut. Since then, the fund has barely moved, trading around $26.
There are other bullish signs surrounding Anthropic's IPO in the derivatives markets. Current prices for perpetual futures on the blockchain exchange Hyperliquid are implying an opening price of $98, a big pop from the $70-$78 price range quoted in the company's amended S1 filing. The AI giant is expected to price Wednesday evening and begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

sources.news_title: Anthropic Opens At $111.5 A Share, 34% Higher Than Its IPO Price Of $83 In Biggest IPO In History
sources.text:
Wall Street had a lot of appetite for the first pure-play AI lab to go public.
Anthropic opened at $111.50 a share in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday. That is about 34% above the $83 price at which it sold shares in its initial public offering the night before. The stock trades under the ticker “ANT”. It started trading just before noon ET, roughly two hours after the market opened, and gave up some of its early gains in the first hour. It was trading around $101, still about 22% above the IPO price.
At the opening price, the maker of Claude has a market capitalization of roughly $2 trillion. That puts a company founded only five years ago among the handful of trillion-dollar public companies in the world.
The Biggest IPO On Record
Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 on Wednesday night, above its marketed range of $70 to $78. Strong demand meant the deal was also upsized from 825 million shares to 980 million. About 956 million of those were sold by the company and the rest by existing stockholders.
The offering raised about $81.3 billion. That makes it the largest IPO on record, ahead of SpaceX’s $75 billion listing in June. Underwriters also have an option to buy another 147 million shares at the IPO price, which could take total proceeds past $93 billion. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led the deal, as they did for SpaceX.
Demand was intense. Bloomberg, citing underwriters, reported that the offering was up to seven times oversubscribed, and only about half of institutional orders were filled. Roughly 20% of the shares were set aside for retail investors through brokerages including E*Trade, Charles Schwab, SoFi and Fidelity.
A Dramatic Re-Rating In Weeks
The pricing was a big step up from where the roadshow began. Earlier this month, the numbers in Anthropic’s filing pointed to a valuation of just over $1.02 trillion at the top of its range, barely above its last private valuation of $965 billion. The final $83 price gave it a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion. At Thursday’s opening price, the market is putting a value of about $2 trillion on the company.
The climb looks even steeper over a longer period. Anthropic raised funds at a $183 billion valuation in September 2025. Barely 14 months later, public investors are valuing it at more than ten times that.
The Numbers Behind The Demand
Investors are betting on revenue growth that has little precedent. Anthropic’s annualized revenue run-rate went from about $1 billion at the start of 2025 to more than $47 billion by May this year, driven mainly by enterprise customers and Claude Code. Ahead of the listing, the company told investors that third-quarter revenue had risen nearly 50% to $16.7 billion, and that it had been profitable on an adjusted basis for two quarters in a row.
The risks are just as large. The prospectus showed that Anthropic lost $42 billion in 2025, though most of that was a non-cash accounting charge. It also has more than $500 billion in cloud and computing commitments in the coming years. The timing was not easy either. Two weeks ago, tech and AI stocks sold off sharply, with the Nasdaq dropping more than 5% in a day. The industry was then shaken again by the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang just before pricing. Neither event seems to have dampened demand for Anthropic’s shares.
Buyers of the stock are also getting limited say in how the company is run. Anthropic’s governance structure leaves control split between a Long-Term Benefit Trust and an LLC owned by its seven co-founders, a setup meant to protect the company’s safety mission once it is public.
How It Compares With SpaceX
Anthropic’s first-day jump is larger than SpaceX’s. When SpaceX listed in June, it priced at $135 and opened at $150, about 11% higher, before closing its first day up about 19%. Anthropic opened 34% above its offer price. SpaceX still holds the record for the largest IPO by valuation, at $1.77 trillion against Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion at the offer price. Anthropic has, however, raised more money.
The listing is also a major payday for the people who built the company. More than half of Anthropic’s roughly 5,300 employees could hold stakes worth at least $10 million, and around 600 could be sitting on stakes worth more than $100 million. Executives such as CFO Krishna Rao and CTO Rahul Patil, who did much of the work behind the listing, will be among those watching the stock closely.
What It Means For AI
Anthropic’s debut is the clearest public-market test so far of whether AI labs can justify the valuations they have reached in private funding rounds. A first-day pop of this size suggests that, for now, public investors are willing to pay even more than private ones did. That will matter to OpenAI, which has yet to announce plans for an IPO. With SpaceX already listed, Anthropic now public and OpenAI possibly to follow, the three companies could together be worth more than every US tech IPO from the last 45 years combined.
The opening day is only the start. SpaceX traded as high as the $220s after its debut and was later trading below its IPO price. Anthropic will now have to justify a $2 trillion price tag every quarter, in public.
